newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Top End sees Asia link in rail line.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Top End sees Asia link in rail line.

text.p: The political leader of the Northern Territory is about to fight for the Top End's future in Asia by making a determined pitch for Federal government backing for a railway link with the rest of Australia.

Chief Minister Shane Stone said in an interview with Reuters that he was more optimistic than ever before that he will win approval for the 1,410 km, A$1 billion rail link between Darwin and Alice Springs.
This was despite a government decision two weeks ago to kill the infrastructure bonds scheme which was to have supported the railway, which is backed by Asian commercial interests.
"Hey, we were wiped out by cyclones and bombed by the Japanese. This is nothing, some politician in Canberra with the stroke of a pen trying to play around with our future," Stone said.
The Northern Territory's (NT) biggest fight is designed to promote its growing Asian links by making Darwin the main port for Australian commodity and manufactured goods exports.

Stone, 46, now in his second year as Chief Minister, agreed that Canberra's concern for its mainstream political base may help explain its lack of support so far for a rail link for the sparsely-populated north.
But the rail link would be good for Australia as a whole and was a matter of keen interest in Asia, he said.
Asia is clearly the key to Stone's view of the future of the NT, with the rail link an important part of the vision.
Every government's minister's office in Darwin displays a huge map of "our region", showing the northern half of Australia and East Asia to China, Korea And Japan.
The long-mooted rail link was a main key to whether the Top End fully realised its vision of becoming the main zone for Australian exports to Asia, Stone said.
Already the NT has built an impressive record of Asian links.
The Territory's mainly commodity exports are estimated to amount to A$1.3 billion in 1996/97, with 90 percent bound for Asia.
With one percent of Australia's population, the Territory has 1.6 percent of its exports, Stone said.

The NT is also effectively part of the East ASEAN Growth Area (EAGA), a "polygon" of the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, part of Kalimantan, the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, Brunei and the Philippine island of Mindanao, he said.
An unofficial member, the NT was invited to EAGA meetings and had signed memorandums of understanding on its links with all states apart from Sabah and Sarawak.
"They don't throw us out," Stone said, in reference to Malaysia's effective exclusion of federal Australian involvement from several regional bodies and meetings in recent years.
But the rail link is the key to how far the Territory's Asian trade ambitions can proceed.
Use of Darwin as a port would save 11 days on a Tokyo-Adelaide shipping run, 12 days on the Surabaya-Melbourne run and seven days on the Singapore-Adelaide run, NT government studies show.
Stone did not disclose details of the proposal he will be taking to Australian Prime Minister John Howard in mid-March.
"I would love to be able to say to the prime minister 'we don't need your help, we can do this on our own'," he said.
But achieving the rail link without the Federal government could only be done with great difficulty, he said.
Korea's Daewoo group, one of the main commercial interests which wish to back the rail link if conditions are right, would probably not go ahead with the project without Federal backing, he said.
But Stone said he took heart from a February 14 statement that Canberra would consider alternative arrangements for continuing its support for "genuine infrastructure investment".
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
